Earlier this year, after rolling out managed accounts for parents of children under 13, WhatsApp is today extending its parental supervision features to teen accounts, adding group activity notifications and additional restrictions on Meta AI. Here are the details.

WhatsApp expands parental supervision options

Earlier this year, WhatsApp announced a series of new features aimed at giving parents greater control over the accounts of children under 13.

These include letting parents decide who can contact that account, as well as which groups the account can join, view message requests from unknown contacts, and manage its privacy settings, with all changes protected by a password set by the parent.

A few weeks ago, WhatsApp further expanded this feature on iOS, adding a dedicated "Parental Supervision" section in the Settings app to make it easier for parents to find and configure managed accounts.

WhatsApp is once again expanding these supervision features today, this time extending parental supervision from children under 13 to teens, while giving parents greater insight into group activity and more say over how their children use channels and status updates—particularly when interacting with Meta AI.

With the update, parents will now receive notifications when their child joins or leaves a group, as well as when an existing group their child is in sees a "significant increase" in membership. Parents can also choose how their child uses channels, whose status updates they can view, and who can see their child's own status updates.

As for Meta AI, parents can now choose between the standard experience designed for users aged 13 and over, and a stricter "Limited Content" option, depending on what they feel is more appropriate for their child.

WhatsApp says the "Limited Content" setting will further restrict the topics teens can discuss with Meta AI. When this setting is enabled, Meta AI features that rely on Private Processing will also become unavailable.

WhatsApp reiterates that these parental supervision features do not give parents access to their children's actual messages or calls, as that content remains protected by end-to-end encryption.
